content: After repeated dosing, the observed mean elimination half-life (t½) of lamivudine ranged from 5 to 7 hours. The mean renal clearance was approximately 1 mL/min (mean ± SD) for doses ranging from 25 to 10 mg/kg. Special Populations The pharmacokinetics of lamivudine were studied in a small group of HIV-1-infected adults with impaired renal function. Exposure to lamivudine, as measured by AUC∞, Cmax, and half-life, increased as renal function declined (assessed by creatinine clearance). The apparent total oral clearance (Cl/F) of lamivudine decreased with decreasing creatinine clearance. Tmax was not significantly affected by renal function. Based on these findings, dosage adjustments of lamivudine are recommended for patients with renal impairment. In a study of otherwise healthy individuals with impaired renal function, hemodialysis increased lamivudine clearance from a mean of 64 mL/min to 88 mL/min. However, the 4-hour duration of hemodialysis was insufficient to significantly alter mean lamivudine exposure after a single dose. Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis and automated peritoneal dialysis had negligible effects on lamivudine clearance. Therefore, after adjusting the dose for creatinine clearance, no additional dose modification is necessary following routine hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. It is unknown whether lamivudine can be removed by continuous (24-hour) hemodialysis. The effects of renal impairment on lamivudine pharmacokinetics in pediatric patients are not known. The pharmacokinetics of lamivudine were studied in adults with impaired hepatic function. Pharmacokinetic parameters were not altered by reduced hepatic function, and no dose adjustment is required for patients with hepatic impairment. The safety and efficacy of lamivudine have not been established in patients with decompensated liver disease. Pediatric Patients In pediatric patients (aged 8 months to 16 years, weight range: 5 to 66 kg) receiving oral and IV doses of 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 20 mg/kg/day, the pharmacokinetics of lamivudine were evaluated. In 9 infants and children (aged 5 months to 12 years) receiving the recommended pediatric dose of 4 mg/kg twice daily as an oral solution, the absolute bioavailability was 66% ± 26% (mean ± SD), which was lower than the 86% ± 16% (mean ± SD) observed in adults. The mechanism for the reduced absolute bioavailability in infants and children is unknown. Systemic clearance decreased with increasing age in pediatric subjects. Total exposure to lamivudine, as reflected by mean AUC values, was comparable between pediatric subjects receiving an 8-mg/kg/day dose and adults receiving a 4-mg/kg/day dose. The distribution of lamivudine into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was assessed in 38 pediatric subjects after multiple oral doses. CSF samples were collected 2 to 4 hours post-dose, and the mean CSF concentration was approximately 0.3 mcg/mL. Limited and uncontrolled pharmacokinetic and safety data are available from the administration of lamivudine (and zidovudine) to 36 infants up to 1 week old in two trials conducted in South Africa. In these trials, lamivudine clearance was substantially reduced in 1-week-old neonates compared to pediatric subjects older than 3 months. There is insufficient information to determine the time course of changes in clearance between the immediate neonatal period and the age ranges beyond 3 months. Geriatric Patients The pharmacokinetics of lamivudine in patients over 65 years of age have not been studied. Drug Interactions No significant pharmacokinetic interaction was observed between lamivudine and interferon alfa in a trial involving 19 healthy male subjects. In vitro data suggest that ribavirin reduces the phosphorylation of lamivudine, stavudine, and zidovudine. However, no clinically significant interaction (e.g., loss of HIV-1/HCV virologic suppression) was observed when ribavirin was coadministered with lamivudine, stavudine, or zidovudine as part of a multidrug regimen in HIV-1/HCV co-infected subjects. Lamivudine and TMP-SMX were coadministered to 14 HIV-1-positive subjects in a single-center, open-label, randomized, crossover trial. Each subject received a single 300-mg dose of lamivudine and TMP 160 mg/SMX 800 mg once daily for 5 days, with concomitant administration of lamivudine 300 mg with the fifth dose in a crossover design.
